hints: Start with what Fig. 3.1 shows - a single monomer that builds up a messenger RNA chain. How many different chemical groups join together to make one of these monomers?

Match shape to chemistry - the six-sided ring at the top contains nitrogen, the five-sided ring in the middle is a five-carbon sugar, and the small circle on the left is an acidic group containing phosphorus.
Remember this is RNA, not DNA, so the middle sugar is the one with an extra oxygen. Name all three groups using the exact syllabus terms for a nucleotide.
walkthrough:
Recognise an RNA nucleotide**
Messenger RNA is a polynucleotide, so its monomer is a ribonucleotide. Every nucleotide is built from the same three parts joined together.

Assign D, E and F**
D is the six-sided ring joined to the sugar - the nitrogenous organic base. E is the five-sided five-carbon sugar, which in RNA is ribose. F is the circle joined to the sugar - the phosphate group.
Final answer: D = nitrogenous base; E = ribose; F = phosphate group.

hints: Think side-by-side: DNA is normally found as a very long double molecule in the nucleus, while messenger RNA is a short single copy made for protein synthesis. Pick just one clear structural contrast.
walkthrough:
Choose one valid structural contrast**
You only need one difference. Good options are: DNA has two strands and mRNA has one, DNA has deoxyribose and mRNA has ribose, DNA has thymine and mRNA has uracil, DNA is a double helix with base pairing and mRNA is single-stranded and longer in DNA than mRNA.
Final answer: DNA has two polynucleotide strands / deoxyribose / thymine / base pairs / double helix, whereas mRNA has one strand / ribose / uracil / no base pairs / straight chain.

hints: Look carefully at Fig. 3.2B - where does the end of the DNA sit inside the telomerase, and what other nucleic acid is already lined up against it?
Recall what an enzyme active site does - it holds substrates close together in the correct orientation. What are the free substrates shown arriving at the top of the diagram?
Think about the rules that decide which free substrate pairs with each position on the template, and what type of strong bond must then join those new units into a chain.
Follow the arrow showing movement of telomerase - what does sliding along allow the enzyme to do next so the telomere gets longer?
walkthrough:
Position the template**
The short template RNA inside telomerase binds to the exposed single-stranded DNA of region X in the enzyme active site. This holds the DNA end steady so new nucleotides can be added.

Add complementary DNA nucleotides**
Free DNA nucleotides align against the RNA by complementary base pairing with hydrogen bonds between bases: A pairs with T, C pairs with G, and U in RNA pairs with A in DNA. Phosphodiester bonds then form between adjacent DNA nucleotides to build the new telomere strand.

Move along to extend further**
Telomerase then slides in the direction of the arrow, to the right, freeing more of the RNA template so further nucleotides can be added. In this way telomerase acts like a reverse transcriptase, making DNA using an RNA template.

Final answer: Template RNA binds in active site of telomerase to region X DNA; free DNA nucleotides pair with RNA by complementary base pairing (A-T, C-G, U-A); phosphodiester bonds form between adjacent DNA nucleotides; telomerase moves to the right to continue elongation.

hints: Think about the shape of the main DNA molecule in a prokaryote compared with the linear chromosomes in eukaryotes - where are telomeres found and why would that shape make them unnecessary?
walkthrough:
Link shape to need**
Telomeres are protective repeating sequences at the ends of linear DNA molecules. Prokaryotic DNA is circular, a continuous loop with no free ends, so there is nothing to shorten during replication and no telomeres to maintain.
Final answer: Prokaryotes have circular DNA with no ends, so they have no telomeres and need no telomerase.

hints: Recall what makes cancer cells different in division - they keep dividing without normal stopping or ageing. What normally happens to telomeres each time a healthy cell divides?
Connect that to enzyme activity - if chromosomes must stay intact through many extra divisions, what does that tell you about the level of telomere-building activity you would expect to detect?
walkthrough:
Why cancer cells need telomere maintenance**
Normal telomeres shorten at each division, which limits cell divisions. Cancer cells divide continuously without ageing, so without repair their chromosomes would shorten and lose genes.

Use telomerase as a marker**
Active telomerase synthesises new telomere DNA and keeps chromosomes intact. Finding high levels of telomerase, or the gene for telomerase switched on, in bronchus lining cells therefore suggests uncontrolled cancerous division.
Final answer: Cancer cells divide continuously / uncontrollably; telomerase prevents chromosome shortening so high telomerase activity indicates cancer cells.
